title: New York Times' Connections: A Case Study on NLP in Word Games — Shafik Quoraishee, NYT Games
talk_summary: An NYT games developer describes independent, preliminary research modeling the Connections word game as an augmented graph-coloring problem, using semantic similarity graphs (WordNet/ConceptNet/embeddings), graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning to generate candidate solutions. The core claim is that structuring the search space with explicit relational metrics beats naive LLM prompting, and that LLM solvability is suspect because puzzle answers exist on the internet.

takeaways.what_they_do: He distrusts LLM solve rates on Connections because the answers are published online, so a high score may reflect memorization rather than reasoning; he builds a non-LLM solver as a comparison baseline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: LLMs often are trained on internet data and the puzzle solutions are available on the internet. So, who knows if they're just pulling the solutions from the internet.

takeaways.technique: Structured relational scoring instead of single similarity score
takeaways.what_they_do: He argues one similarity metric is insufficient; he computes multiple relational-alignment scores (semantic, morphological, encyclopedic, associative) and combines them into a multi-dimensional profile per item.

takeaways.technique: Explicit relationship graph as search-space reduction
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of dumping 16 words into an LLM, he precomputes edges (relationship strengths) between items so the solver searches a constrained candidate space rather than the full combinatorial one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Without that it's falling into the random range ... it becomes much more difficult.
takeaways.numbers: Random guessing from full board ~0% win; after one category solved ~1/5000; with two solved ~1/35.

takeaways.what_they_do: A graph neural network proposes candidate subgraphs, then a reinforcement-learning system navigates/selects among them, rather than one model producing a final answer in one shot.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the graph neural network that's actually outputting candidate graphs ... then you find out which graph like fits into the candidate solutions.

takeaways.what_they_do: He builds a deterministic graph/algorithmic solver to handle the structured part of the problem, reserving LLM reasoning only where structure can't be encoded.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I'm not just doing a reasoning model or dumbly putting into an LLM. I'm actually trying to increase this intelligence space like procedurally.
